title: The Investment Consequences Of The US-Canada Trade Spat
text:
The Investment Consequences Of The US-Canada Trade Spat

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research
| 24 Aug 2026

Unlike European leaders, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney elected to walk away from what he felt was a bad trade deal for his country. In time, this could end up having an important political cost for him. Ontario, the industrial heartland of Canada but also the core base of Carney’s Liberal Party, will likely bear the brunt of the economic fallout of the breakdown in US-Canadian trade. So why would Carney take such a risk? There are many possible explanations.

The first, and strongest, explanation is that Carney’s decision was driven by the shifting geopolitical landscape. The deal the US put on the table, one which involved Canada essentially turning its back on China, a rapidly growing trade partner, would have left Canada as essentially an economic dominion of the United States. This would be hard to swallow even at the best of times, and with the best of allies. But obviously the US in the past few quarters has hardly been the best of allies to Canada; the US president choosing to describe the prime minister as a governor, calling the country a 51st state, talking about invading Greenland, or encouraging Albertan secession... Against such a backdrop, it is perhaps not that surprising that Carney was not that enthusiastic about tying his country’s economic fortunes ever more closely to those of a US whose political decision-making process appears increasingly both aggressive and unpredictable. After all, if Canada agreed today to sever economic ties with China, who is to say what the US might ask for tomorrow? Sever ties with Europe should President Trump become angry at the European Union? With Brazil if President Trump changes his mind about President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva?... After all, the USMCA agreement was renegotiated from Nafta just seven years ago and at the time, Trump described it as the best of deals. In that regards, Carney’s quip that “we recognized that sometimes the US signature is written in pencil” is a powerful line that will likely be remembered for a long time to come.
The second explanation might be politically driven. Sure, the trade war with the US will unleash some economic costs on Canada and in time this could prove politically damaging for Carney. But at the same time, standing up to what is now perceived in Canada as US bullying could, at least in the short term, prove to be politically positive for Carney. On this, a personal anecdote: my two daughters attend boarding school on Vancouver Island and I was recently there, buying oranges at the local grocery store before one of their rugby matches (orange quarters at half time being a rugby tradition; unless one is called Serge Blanco, in which case half time is a pack of Marlboro reds). As I was picking up oranges, a lady of a certain age (i.e. past 80, Vancouver Island being the land of the newly-weds and nearly-deads) came up to me and said “you can’t buy these. They are from California!”. A defiance against US products which is starting to come through in the data. Indeed, while Canadian imports of US goods (whether planes, Caterpillar machines, chemical products etc…) stand at record highs, the past 18 months have witnessed a clear drop in the imports of consumer products. A stealth boycott of US goods amongst Canadian consumers does seem to be taking place.

This shift in Canadian attitudes to the US could have a silver lining. Canada’s main comparative advantage is to get things out of the ground (whether oil, natural gas, gold, wheat, potash...) in a jurisdiction investors feel broadly comfortable with. Against that, Canada has, in recent years, proven particularly incompetent in building the infrastructure that would allow local commodity producers to maximize revenues in the international market, whether an oil pipeline from Alberta to the BC ports, LNG terminals in the Maritimes that would allow Canada to sell more natural gas to a gas-thirsty Western Europe... Instead, Canadian producers have had to sell discounted oil, electricity or natural gas to the only easily accessible market, namely the US. All of which brings us to the silver lining of the current US-Canadian trade spat. By shutting the American door, and wrapping himself in the Maple-Leaf flag, Carney has now made it much harder for the various groups (Greens, First Nations, New Democratic Party local governments…) who have so far stood in the way of the required infrastructure, to keep blocking the pipelines, railroads and LNG terminals that will, in time allow Canadian producers to reap higher rewards. Essentially, Mark Carney can now steamroll anyone standing in the way of the much-needed infrastructure roll-out with the “patriotic card.” If he manages to do so, Carney could still go down as a consequential Canadian prime minister. If he does not, then the combination of the lack of Canadian infrastructure roll-out and the breakdown of the relationship with the US would leave Canada in tough economic binds. High stakes…
Another interesting angle to the US-Canada spat will be the response of Canadian pension funds. The “Big Nine” Canadian pension funds (i.e. CPPIB, La Caisse, BCI, AIMCO, Ontario Teachers…) collectively manage around CAD2.5trn and it is estimated that around half of that money is deployed in the US. This asset allocation mostly reflects the fact that the US offers a depth of capital markets that no other country can match. Nevertheless, if given the opportunity, Canadian pension funds would most likely be happier deploying capital at home rather than abroad; especially now given the overall political context. All of which brings us back to the needed infrastructure spending mentioned above (whether pipelines, railroads, LNG terminals...). The reality is that Canadian capital very much exists to fund this infrastructure. What has lacked so far has been the political will to make this happen. If the political will is now found, capital could return to Canada, instead of constantly leaving. This would eventually turn bullish for the loonie?

All of which brings us to the investment consequences of the US-Canadian fallout. From a quick glance across the weekend’s financial media, the consensus take seems to be that the US-Canadian trade spat is inherently bearish for the Canadian dollar and Canadian assets. To be sure, trade wars, especially between friends, are always regrettable and do not deliver good outcomes. From a US standpoint, this trade war is also poorly timed given the looming US-China summit, and the unfolding consequences of the US-Iran war (i.e. soaring diesel prices, rising freight costs...). So, to the extent that the Canadian dollar and Canadian assets tend to be rather cyclical, the initial consensus reaction makes ample sense; over the coming weeks, Canadian asset prices, and the loonie, may well trade on the heavy side. But over the long term, if the current trade spat does provide the needed electroshock for Canada to finally roll-out its commodity infrastructure, and if this infrastructure is funded by Canadian pension funds repatriating some assets from the US, then the longer-term impact should then prove to be very bullish for Canadian commodity-producing assets, and for the Canadian dollar.

Finally, another interesting angle to Mark Carney’s decision to slam the door in President Trump’s face is the image that this will portray of Canada to the rest of the world, and especially to China. This matters because until 2018, Chinese investors had been keen buyers of Canadian assets (it’s not for nothing that Vancouver is sometimes referred to as Hongcouver). But this appetite for Canadian assets stalled with the arrest of Meng Wanzhou (the Huawei CFO) and the sudden perception that, when it came to tensions between the US and China, Canada would always side with the US. This made Canadian assets a lot less attractive to Chinese buyers. To the extent that this perception now shifts again, the loonie could suddenly find a Chinese, and foreign, bid once again?
